nameStory: The "three-square" name comes from the plant's distinctive triangular stem that feels sharply three-sided when you roll it between your fingers. Unlike round-stemmed rushes, this bulrush's stem has three distinct edges that form a triangle in cross-section, making it feel almost like a tiny green ruler.
description: Three-square bulrush is a sturdy wetland plant that looks like a cluster of tall, dark green pencils poking up from the water's edge. It grows 1-4 feet tall with distinctive triangular stems that have sharp edges you can actually feel. The stems are topped with small, brownish flower clusters that appear in mid to late summer. This tough sedge forms colonies along shorelines and in shallow water throughout New England.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Roll the stem between your thumb and finger - it feels sharply three-sided like a tiny triangle, not round or flat. The three edges are distinct and can feel almost cutting.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small brown clusters appear near the top of stems in summer, looking like tiny brown pompoms or bristly balls about the size of a pea.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very few leaves, and they're much shorter than the stems - often just small sheaths at the base that you might overlook entirely.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in clumps or colonies of upright stems that emerge directly from the water or wet soil, like a bunch of green straws stuck in the mud.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Stems feel firm and solid, not squishy or hollow like some wetland plants. They're tough enough that they won't crush easily in your hand.

habitat: Look for three-square bulrush in shallow water and along the muddy edges of ponds, marshes, and slow streams throughout New England. It thrives in brackish areas where fresh and salt water mix, making it common in coastal marshes and tidal areas. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, arrowhead, and other water-loving sedges in areas that flood regularly.

seasonality.spring: New green triangular shoots emerge from the mud and shallow water, growing rapidly as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and produce their characteristic brown flower clusters from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Stems begin to turn brown and the seed heads mature and release seeds, though the triangular stems remain sturdy.
seasonality.winter: Dead brown stems often persist above the waterline, and you can still feel the three-sided shape even in dried stems.

funFact: Three-square bulrush is like nature's multi-tool - Indigenous peoples used its tough triangular stems to weave baskets so strong they could hold water, and the stems were even used as needles for sewing because of their sharp, rigid edges.
confusionNotes: Other bulrushes in the area have round stems that feel smooth when rolled between your fingers, while three-square's triangular stem is unmistakable. Remember: "Three-square has three sharp sides" - if it doesn't feel triangular, it's a different bulrush species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "bulrush," this plant is actually a sedge, not a true rush. The "bulrush" name is a common term for several different wetland plants, which can be confusing. Sedges have the triangular stems ("sedges have edges"), while true rushes typically have round stems.
compareHints: Among its bulrush relatives, three-square is the only one with the distinctive triangular stem - soft-stemmed bulrush has round, squishy stems, while hardstem bulrush has round, firm stems. American three-square bulrush is very similar but tends to be found in more brackish, coastal areas and has slightly different flower arrangements.

Water bulrush stands apart from other bulrushes by its aquatic lifestyle and incredibly thin stems.
Among New England's bulrushes, hardstem bulrush is distinguished by its exceptional height and remarkably rigid stems.
Among New England bulrushes, Torrey's is distinguished by its moderate triangular stems that aren't as sharply angled as three-square bulrush or as round as soft-stemmed bulrush.
American three-square bulrush is distinguished from its bulrush relatives by its sharply triangular stems and salt-tolerant habitat.

Among its bulrush relatives, slender bulrush stands out for its perfectly cylindrical stems - three-square bulrush and American three-square bulrush both have distinctly triangular stems you can feel with your fingers.
Common club-rush stands out from other New England bulrushes by having perfectly round, completely leafless stems.
